name: Beryl-Tempest
description: Beryl-Tempest is a sea of green-gold water under a sky of banded storm, wrapped by the Tempest—a hurricane belt circling the entire equator like a ring of white fire. North and south of the belt, the ocean runs warm and kind; within it, waves stack forty meters high beneath lightning that never stops. Beneath the seafloor everywhere lies a second ocean, sealed and dark, its tides measurable only as faint tremors in the crust.

The dense air carries sound enormous distances: whale-song from the polar herds arrives at the equator days later, and sailors swear the storms sing back. At night the sea glows where vast schools of lantern-fish migrate, tracing currents in rivers of blue-green fire that mirror the auroras above.

The oceanographic platform Windlass has studied the lantern-fish for nine years from the storm belt's southern edge—and for nine years has quietly failed to explain their navigation, which tracks a point deep beneath the crust with more precision than any instrument aboard. Twelve years before Windlass anchored, the survey station Halcyon Spire lost orbit in this same sea; her hulk still transmits housekeeping telemetry on a schedule no one set, from an altitude that should have decayed years ago.

Lantern-fish biomass regenerates cardiac tissue and sells for fortunes, but harvest crews now refuse contracts north of the Tempest, where three ships have been lost without debris and the fish gather in spirals kilometers wide—always counterclockwise, always centered on open water above the buried ocean's deepest point. The spiral moved last month. Windlass's director has stopped filing reports on where it went.
